transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Order of the Dry Saint [F-02].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain needles down on grey water as your boat noses up to the last dry stone of the Ashwater Causeway. A knot of soaked, silent refugees huddles behind you — all that's left of a hamlet the river finally took. Ahead, torchlight gutters at the toll-gate, where a handful of Wardens in rain-slick leather stand chains-ready, more frightened than fierce, eyeing the crowd for any sign of the fever-shake that means hive-touched. Somewhere behind the gate smoke already rises — they've started burning a house. The gate captain steps forward, hand on his chain-hook, and asks the question that decides who crosses tonight and who doesn't.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Captain, let me check them first. I hear things before they show—if any soul here carries the fever-song, I'll hear it. You have my word on that.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra moves between the refugees and the gate, hands visible and palms open. She stands tall despite her soaked clothes, making herself into the thing they need to focus on instead of their panic.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Captain, they're not touched. I've cleared hive-fever for years. Tell me what you need to see.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward through the rain, meeting the captain's eyes. Something in his weathered bearing—the way he moves, unhurried and certain—suggests he knows what he's looking for. He glances back at the huddle of refugees once, a practiced assessment.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I'm Caddock. I've pulled more fever-sick children from their mothers' arms than you've drawn breath, Captain. If there's blight-touched in this group, I'll smell it before your chain-hooks ever twitch. These folk are sound. Let them through.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock pushes forward through the huddle of refugees, rain-slick and steady. She plants herself between the nervous crowd and the Warden Captain, one hand resting on her medical bag. Her eyes meet his without a trace of the fear that's poisoning the air around them.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Captain Ossa — I can help you check them. I know the sickness when I see it, and I know these folk. None of them carry the fever-shake.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps from the boat into the causeway rain, shoulders broad and soaked. His militia cloak swings heavy as he moves toward the gate with the bearing of a guard who never truly left his post. He positions himself as the buffer between the frightened refugees and the chain-ready Wardens, meeting Captain Ossa's eyes directly — not challenging, but solid. Present. Still holding the line.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Captain Ossa lets the silence stretch, chain-hook tapping once against his palm as he studies four strangers all vouching at once — a toll-keeper's daughter, a self-taught fever-reader, a midwife with steel in her spine, and a man who still stands like he wears the militia colors. Behind him the smoke from the burning house thickens, and somewhere down the line a Warden mutters about quotas and torches. Ossa finally lowers the hook, jerks his chin toward the gate. "Fine. One at a time, hands out, mouths open — Anselm, you're checking, since you claim the eye for it. Caddock, second opinion. Petra, Yarrow — you two are vouching with your names, and Ossa doesn't forget names." The refugees shuffle forward under torchlight, rain hissing off hot iron, and for now the chains stay slack — but the gate isn't open yet, only unlocked.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No fever-song. Not one of them carries it, Captain.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra stands motionless among the shuffling refugees, her senses opening to the frequencies only she perceives. Her head tilts slightly as she listens through the rain and the crowd's anxious murmur, scanning for the telltale buzz of the swarm-song that would mark hive-touched flesh. After a long moment she straightens, meeting Captain Ossa's gaze with quiet certainty.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: No fever-shake. No burst wells. No swarm-song in the breath. He's clear.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps into the torchlight without hesitation, rain streaming off his coat. He motions the first refugee forward, his movements economical and practiced—hands firm but not rough as he tips the person's chin up to check the whites of their eyes, studies their palms for the telltale tremor, leans close to listen to their breathing. He works through each person methodically, a man who has done this countless times before, his weathered hands steady despite the cold rain.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hand out, steady. I've seen blight-fever turn children grey from the inside out—if it was working on you, I'd smell the rot long before it showed in your eyes.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps forward to the first refugee in line, her movements efficient and assured. She takes their hand with practiced confidence, examines their nails and the whites of their eyes in the torchlight, checks their pulse, leans close to smell their breath and skin for any sign of blight corruption. Her fingers are steady, her assessment quick and certain.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Easy now — just step forward with your hands clear and your voice steady. The Captain's doing what needs doing.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow stands at the threshold of the checking line, his broad frame a bulwark against the rain. As each refugee steps forward toward Anselm's scrutiny, he nods them onward with quiet certainty. His militia bearing seems to settle the frightened crowd—not hope, but purpose. Still holding the line.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No fever-song. Not one of them carries it, Captain.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra refuses a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Notice: dice + 0 + - → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text:
Petra plants her feet and says it a second time, flat and certain — "No fever-song. Not one of them." She won't soften it into a plea for Ossa's mercy, and that refusal costs her: she digs a fate point from her purse as, faint under the hiss of rain and the crackle of the burning house behind the gate, a thread of the swarm-song rises — H-02's promise that it *calls* — just enough that two refugees flinch and Ossa's hand twitches back toward his chain-hook. But Petra doesn't flinch. Her read is dead accurate and she says it with such flat authority that the whole line settles at once; refugees who'd been shaking stop shaking, and even the nervous Wardens ease off their hooks. Ossa's jaw works, but he can't argue with what his own eyes are now telling him — no rot, no tremor, no grey creeping up anyone's throat. The aspect **No Fever-Song Among Them** sits solid over the whole group now, hers to lean on again if anyone questions it. Anselm and Caddock finish clearing the rest of the line without complication, and the gate chains go still.

Ossa exhales, spits once into the flood-water, and steps back. "Fine. Through. All of them." He looks past you at the smoke rising off the burning house down the causeway. "But you four — Hollowmoot's asking who's coming up the road, and I'd rather it be someone who can vouch for what's *behind* you too. Something's got the swarm-song loud tonight. Louder than it's been in weeks." He doesn't unchain the gate fully — just enough for the column to file through, single file, into the dark.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I promised Vex I would repay her life-debt by answering when she called in a favor, no matter the cost. She says one of her people—a smuggler she swore to shield—is trapped with the refugees.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Vex pulled me from the cellars. I don't refuse debts.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'Favor of Blackwater Lieutenant Vex'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Lieutenant Vex of the Blackwater Cartel, soaked to the bone and stripped of her usual swagger, corners Anselm at the gate — the debt she owes him has finally come due, and she's calling it in not for coin but for names she loves. begs the party to go to a half-drowned Stiltfolk watch-camp in the reed maze below the temple, the last post that can still read the coming floods before the water swallows the low channels for good, because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Vex presses a sodden strip of oilcloth into Anselm's hand — a Cartel marker, the kind smugglers use to buy passage through water nobody else can read — and points north past the gate-torches to where the reeds swallow the causeway's light. "The watch-camp's half under already," she says, voice cracking on the word *son*. "Kest is eleven. He heard the bell and he *went*, Anselm, straight into the reeds like something had him by the collar." Behind her, refugees press close for warmth as the rain keeps coming, and somewhere out past the last dry stone, a Stiltfolk lookout's lantern gutters — the only living marker of a path the flood hasn't taken yet. The party has until dark to reach the camp before the low channels close for good and whatever trail is left goes under with them.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear the song that pulled him. I know that call—I know what it means. But I know this water better than anyone here, and I can read the paths before they close. Let's move, now.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra closes her eyes for a moment, listening past the rain and the refugees' voices. The swarm-song threads through the night—Kest's pull into the reeds, down toward the flood. She knows that call. But she forces herself still, gathering the knowledge that's lived in her bones since childhood: the water speaks, and she hears it. She approaches the causeway's edge where the reeds part slightly, studying the current and the light on the channels, reading how the flood opens certain paths and closes others with each surge.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I owe you the debt, Vex. I'll find your boy.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm takes the oilcloth marker from Vex's hand, feeling its weight. He doesn't offer false comfort or promises beyond what he means. He turns to study the reed maze beyond the gate-torches, letting his eyes trace the half-drowned path north. The swarm-song he heard at the causeway still echoes somewhere in his bones—the same song that took his sister. This time, he knows what he's hunting.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: A child lost to the swarm-song? Then we don't waste breath on planning—we move now. I've delivered babies in floods that would drown lesser folk. I know how to read a rising water and keep a frightened child breathing in the dark. Give me that marker, Vex. We'll bring him home.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock immediately starts moving with quiet purpose, checking her satchel for rope, oil, clean water—everything a frightened child might need to survive the swamp and weather. There's no hesitation in her, no moment of doubt. She looks directly at Vex, then to Anselm, with the same calm focus she brings to any delivery.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The Stiltfolk won't turn away a Cartel marker, and they'll remember my kin. Brack reads what's under the reeds better than eyes can trust. The boy went toward high ground chasing the song—we find him before the water does. Who's coming?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow calls Brack from the shadows and steps into the torchlight, reading the situation with the practised eye of someone who once held a line. He kneels to ready his hound—a signal that he's preparing to move immediately into the reed maze. His hand rests on Brack's shoulder as he speaks, steadying himself as much as his companion. The rain pounds down, and he's already thinking in channels and currents, in the old knowledge of waterways his family guarded. He waits for the others to commit.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear my name in the song, but I won't answer it. I know these waters better than I know the swarm. Now move—the paths won't hold open much longer.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra refuses a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Notice: dice + - - - → Fair (+2) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The song curls around Petra's own name, soft and wet as a held breath — and she doesn't answer it. She plants her feet against the pull, eyes shut, and reads the water instead: the surge-lines, the drowned camber of old channels, the seams where the flood hasn't yet closed its fist. When she opens her eyes she already has the route traced in her mind, sharp as a scar. "There," she says, pointing past the last torch to a gap in the reeds only she could have seen. "That's our line before the water takes it." Anselm grips Vex's oilcloth marker, Caddock shoulders her satchel, Yarrow sets Brack loose ahead to test the footing — and the four of them step off the last dry stone of the Causeway into the dark, the swarm-song fading behind them under rain and reed-hiss, replaced by something worse: silence, and the sucking pull of water that wants to close behind them.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Stay close and mirror my steps—where I go, the water still holds. Any other way and we're drowned.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra wades into the lead, her feet finding the barely-submerged paths her eyes and ears have already mapped out. She reads the water like language—the seep of it where the ground is firm, the hungry pull where channels open into drowning depths. She calls back sharp hand signals to Anselm, Caddock, and Yarrow, pointing out which way to step, where to push off, where the reeds themselves will betray them. Her whole body is still listening to the swarm-song in the distance, but she keeps her focus on the paths that won't close.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps into the reed maze with the others, one hand gripping the oilcloth marker Vex gave him. He reads the water as he moves—the old mill-channels from his childhood still shape these drowned currents. He stays alert and quiet, ears tuned for Kest's voice or the swarm-song. His sister drowned to that song years ago. This boy won't.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I know this water. We move together and we don't look back.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps into the water without hesitation, feet sure on submerged ground, body angled against the current like she was born to this. She reads the water's pull and mood with her whole frame—where it's safest, how it wants to move them—and checks rope at every person's waist, positioning herself to catch anyone who slips. She moves with the calm competence of someone who has delivered babies in far worse than rain and rising darkness.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Brack reads clean here—no song on this way. Follow my line.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow sends Brack ranging ahead through the reeds, watching how the hound moves with purpose but without panic. Where there's hive-touched danger, Brack will signal—tail down, ears back, a low warning rumble. But the dog moves confident through the brackish water, testing each step, his nose working the air and the murk. Yarrow keeps pace, reading the current with a weir-keeper's practiced eye, feeling how the flood wants to move and where it hasn't yet closed its grip. He marks the safe passage with a low, steady whistle.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice 0 + 0 + → Fantastic (+6) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — create advantage with Physique: dice - 0 - -, invoking Can deliver a child in the dark, silent [CA-03] → Good (+3) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice - - + + → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's line holds true — where she points, the mud stays firm, and the flood's hungry mouth stays shut just long enough. Caddock keeps a hand of rope at every waist, steady as a midwife's grip, and no one so much as stumbles (*Steady Through the Flood*). Ahead, Brack surges through the black water with his ears up and tail loose — no warning growl, no hive-stink on the air — and Yarrow reads that clear as a shout: *Safe Ground Ahead*. The four of you break from the reeds faster than the water wanted to let you, and there, strung between two leaning stilts on the last dry hump of ground, a lantern gutters — a Stiltfolk lookout, watching the channels close behind you. He's already risen to his feet at the sound of your approach, pole in hand, eyes narrow with the wariness of a people who trust no one from the dry roads. Somewhere past him, faint under the rain, the swarm-song still threads through the belltower's silence, and Kest is still out there.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: A boy named Kest heard the swarm-song and followed it into the reeds. Vex of the Cartel sent us with her mark to bring him home before the flood closes the channels for good. Which way did he go?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward with quiet confidence, water streaming from her clothes. She shows proper respect for the lookout's ground but no submission—her eyes and the steady path she just cut through the flood speak for themselves. She keeps listening with that uncanny ear, tracking any shift in the swarm-song's direction past the stilts, reading the air the way she reads water.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: We're here for Kest—the boy who answered the bell. Vex sent us with her marker. We mean no harm to your camp or your people.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps forward with her hands visible and open, keeping her movements deliberate and slow. Her eyes find the lookout's face with the steady, unflinching attention she brings to any frightened person—assessment without judgment. She reaches into her satchel and produces the oilcloth marker Vex pressed into Anselm's hand, holding it out where the guttering lantern catches it. Her whole posture says calm competence: the same stillness she brings to a birth in a storm.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I'm Yarrow, of the Weir-Keepers—you knew my kin. We've come for Kest, who followed the swarm-song into the belltower. Vex sent us to bring him home.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps into the lantern's light with Brack at his side, moving with the steady calm of someone who once held a line and knows how to move through threat. He keeps his hands visible and open, reading the lookout's wariness not as rejection but as righteous caution. When he speaks his family name, it carries weight—these Stiltfolk remember the Weir-Keepers, remember that his blood once guarded these very channels. His posture speaks it: he's soaked through, he's urgent, but he's here with purpose, not panic, and the old knowledge still lives in how he reads the water around them.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The lookout's pole doesn't come up. He looks at the oilcloth marker in Caddock's palm, then at Yarrow's dripping face, and something in his shoulders loosens — not trust, not yet, but recognition. "Weir-Keeper blood still owes us water-debts," he mutters, then jerks his chin north past the last stilt-house toward a black gap in the reeds where the swarm-song threads thinnest but loudest, straight up out of the flood. "Boy went through there near dusk, walking like he was asleep. Belltower's still got two dry rungs left on the ladder — past that, it's the bell's business, not ours." He won't come further himself; the camp's already half underwater and his own people need the lantern kept lit. But he gives Yarrow the line his kin once kept — the last safe channel before the flood closes it for the night — and presses a coil of waxed cord into Petra's hands, Stiltfolk-make, "for the climbing, not the water." The party has their path now: through the gap, to the belltower, to Kest — and whatever answered when he went in.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The toll-house is stone-built, weathered grey, the bell-tower still standing though the paint's gone and the east dock's rotted through. The cellar floods most seasons now, but the upper rooms stay dry. Petra knows every toll-taker on the Causeway; she grew up between their posts and learned to ring the bell before she learned about taxes. She reads the flood-water damage in the stone like she reads weather patterns. The Wardens won't search because they know what she is to this place—someone who's called them home through worse. You don't search the house of someone who's saved your life.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The Wardens know me. I've rung them home before—they won't search this place.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra refuses the compel on 'Raised at the Ashwater Tollgate'.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I delivered him with these hands. From the moment he came out, I knew something was wrong—I could see it in him, feel it in the cord, the wrong-colored flush of his skin. But admitting that would mean admitting my hands failed, and I've spent my entire life building the belief that my hands never fail. To speak it aloud would be to shatter who I am. So I said nothing, not even to myself.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Just the house settling. The timbers always do that when the water rises this high—it's the old wood loosening in the flood. Nothing to be concerned about.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Oath: My Hands Have Never Lost a Child'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Shelter at The shelter is the old tollgate keeper's house at Hollowmoot's edge, Petra's own childhood roof — the Wardens still wave travelers past its door on the strength of her free passage token, never thinking to look inside. hides It hides a birth gone wrong: weeks back Caddock delivered a child in that loft who came out hive-marked, and Cannot Admit Fault, Even to Save a Life — she will not say her hands ever lost one to the blight, so she's kept the boy hidden up there ever since, tending him alone in the dark rather than confess it..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The tollhouse door sticks with damp before it gives, and warmth from a banked fire spills out into the rain — someone's kept this place lived-in. Petra leads you up past the flooded cellar to the dry rooms above, already reciting the Wardens' habits, why no one checks this door. Then a sound from the loft: not rats, not wind. A thin, wrong-rhythmed breathing, and under it, almost too soft to catch, the ghost of a tune. Caddock goes very still on the stairs, her steady hands suddenly not so steady, and the timber-settling story dies in her throat as everyone looks up at once. In the loft, half-swaddled in old sailcloth, a boy no older than three watches you with the flat, patient eyes of the hive-touched — fed, clean, cared for, and utterly hidden from the world.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: How many weeks, Caddock? And more—how much of him is still listening in there, and how much is just the swarm singing through him?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra moves up into the loft without hesitation, her attention already stretching toward the boy. She's listened to the swarm-song long enough to know when it's calling through someone else's throat. She doesn't look away from his flat, patient eyes—she reads him the way she reads water patterns, feeling for where the boy ends and the blight begins.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: How long?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps to the base of the loft stairs and studies the child with the careful attention of an exorcist reading the signs of blight—observing the flat eyes, the wrong-colored flush, the way the boy holds himself. He doesn't speak immediately, just watches.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: He's no threat to any of you. He's fed and clean and kept from harm—kept from becoming harm to anyone else.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock climbs into the loft and positions herself between the group and the hive-marked boy, one hand on his shoulder. Her usual midwife's composure has fractured into something harder, more defensive. She refuses to step aside or explain how the child came to be here.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Caddock, how long has he been like this? And how much of the blight is in him?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow stops on the stairs, reading the situation with a militia guard's careful eye. He doesn't panic or retreat; Brack's lack of warning keeps him steady. He addresses Caddock directly, his voice calm and measured, asking the hard question no one else will ask first — how far has the blight taken the boy, and how long has he been hidden. His hands stay open at his sides, not reaching for weapons, not recoiling from the child.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: He's *fine*—he's fine, can't you see he's fine? He's quiet because he's content, not because—he's been fed and kept clean and he hasn't *hurt* anyone. That's all that matters.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock's denial cracks on the word "fine" — her voice breaks, and for one bare second the midwife who has never lost a child looks like a woman who has been drowning in silence for weeks. She doesn't step aside, but she doesn't stop them looking either; her hand stays locked on the boy's shoulder while the truth sits naked in the room. Yarrow's quiet question gets no real answer, only Caddock's ragged insistence that fed and clean and unhurt are the same as safe — and Brack, at the foot of the stairs, still hasn't growled once, watching the boy with more patience than alarm. The swarm-song thins to almost nothing under the child's breathing, like it's listening back. Whatever the party decides now — to hide him deeper, to bring him to the Order, to tell the Wardens, to try to cure him — the choice is theirs alone; Caddock has run out of story to tell them.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The Warden's calling his debt. I said I'd come. Blood-oath to a Weir-Keeper's word.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Cursed to Keep Every Promise Made'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain sheets sideways across the causeway stones as you come down off the tollhouse steps, Kest's fever-weight slung between Caddock's shoulder and Anselm's arm, his breath rattling in that thin, wrong rhythm none of you want to name. At the gate, torchlight gutters on wet chain-links — and it's Ossa himself standing there, hook loose in his hand, water dripping off a brow that's already read the shape of what you're carrying. He doesn't shout the alarm. He looks at Yarrow first, the way a man looks at someone he's still deciding whether to trust. "Weir-Keeper," he says, low enough the others behind him don't catch it over the rain. "Tell me that's a fever and not what I think it is." Somewhere behind you, faint under the storm, the swarm-song threads through the reeds again, patient, certain, calling.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear the fever-song on him, Ossa. Clear as a bell-pattern. We're moving north now.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward from behind the others, her head tilted like she's listening to something threading beneath the rain-noise. She meets Ossa's eyes directly, and when she speaks her certainty is absolute - the kind that comes from hearing what no one else can.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: It's fever, Ossa. I've handled fever. He stays with me.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock doesn't break stride or look back. She keeps her arm around Kest, shielding him, walking toward the gate with the unwavering certainty of a woman who refuses to stop and refuses to admit that anything is wrong.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: He's fever-sick, not hive-touched. But the song knows his name now, Ossa—we move or we lose him to it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow moves to where Kest hangs fevered between the others, stepping into the torchlight to see the boy's face clearly. He reads it the way he reads water—fever-bright eyes, that wrong-rhythm breathing—the child is burning with sickness, not the hive's cold touch. When he straightens and meets Ossa's gaze, his whole body is already turned toward the north, toward the gate. Behind them both, another thread of the swarm-song winds through the rain, patient and certain.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I know fever when I feel it, Ossa. This boy has fever, and he's coming with me.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Ossa's eyes go from Yarrow to Caddock to the boy's rattling breath, and for one long moment the chain-hook doesn't move at all. Then he looks at Yarrow again — not Petra, not Caddock, *Yarrow* — because a Weir-Keeper's word still means something on this stretch of stone. "Fever," Ossa says at last, flat, like he's choosing to believe it because the alternative costs him more than he has left to spend. He steps aside, chain dragging wet across the stones, but his hand closes hard on Yarrow's shoulder as the others pass. "You vouched it. That's yours now, not mine — if I hear different, I come looking for *you* first." It's the promise made in anger's twin, binding tighter than any oath sworn calm, and Yarrow feels the weight of it settle like a second chain. Behind you the gate groans shut, torchlight shrinking to a smear in the rain, and the swarm-song's thread finally goes quiet — for now. Caddock doesn't loosen her grip on Kest until the tollhouse lights are long swallowed by the dark, her jaw set against the truth she still won't say out loud, and somewhere back at Wick Lane, word of a Warden's bent knee tonight will travel faster than any of you would like.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: You've barely cleared the tollgate when the smell hits — pitch smoke, not woodsmoke, rolling low over the water. Ahead, where Petra meant to cut straight through Miller's Row, a knot of Wardens in oilskins are burning an infected house, torches to the stilts of a place someone marked hive-touched, its owner screaming from a boat that two men hold back at spear's length. There's no going through that; the lane's full of Wardens with itchy nerves and lit brands, and Kest's ragged breathing isn't waiting for anyone's patience. You'll have to go around, into water even Petra doesn't like the look of, deeper and colder, with the boy's weight dragging at Anselm's and Caddock's arms every stroke of the way.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Around—through the deep water. I'm reading a track through it.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra turns to study the dark water beyond the burning house, reading the surge-lines and current patterns beneath the surface. Her eyes track across the flooded terrain, searching for the track that stays firm enough—the one that will take them around Miller's Row and clear of the Wardens' attention.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: We'll make it through.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm tightens his grip on Kest's arm and settles deeper into the water's edge, already measuring the currents pulling at his legs. His eyes fix on the darker water ahead, finding the seams where the old mill-roads still run beneath the flood—channels only someone who swam them in better days would know.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hold him high, Anselm. He's no heavier than a newborn after a long labor, and I've waded swamps worse than this—we're going straight through, now.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock braces her legs against the cold current, muscles burning as she powers through water that's already chest-deep. She keeps one hand locked on Kest's shoulder and the other reaching back toward the rope-line, holding the group steady. No stumbling. No hesitation. She's pulled children into the world through worse—and she's not leaving this one to the water or the Wardens' fire.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: There's a way through here. I can feel it in the water. Trust me, and follow close.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow leans forward to the bow, one hand trailing the dark water. His weathered face goes still and intent, reading the subtle play of current against resistance—the way the flood resists certain ground it shouldn't, how the old embankments still shape what wants to drown them. Behind the burning pitch-smoke and the Wardens with their lit brands, here in the spray and cold, he's listening. His jaw tightens. Somewhere beneath this dark surface that terrifies Petra, the water still remembers the channels his family walked.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: It's singing my name. I can't—I can't hold it.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice 0 - 0 + → Great (+4) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — overcome with Physique: dice - - 0 0 → Fair (+2) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice 0 - + -, invoking Reads water-flow like other men read faces [YA-03] → Superb (+5) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The swarm-song wraps around Petra's name like a hand closing over her mouth, and for one terrible breath she stops dead, eyes glazing, feet rooted in the current — then she wrenches free of it, reads the water instead of the song, and traces a line through the deep so clean and sure that even the flood seems to hold still for her (Success With Style). Caddock plows straight through the chest-deep cold behind her, Kest's weight braced against her shoulder like she's carried heavier through worse labors, and she doesn't lose her footing once. At the bow, Yarrow leans out over the black water, one hand trailing the surface, and finds what his family always found here — the ghost of an old channel, firmer ground hidden under eleven years of flood, and he calls it out to the others (Success With Style, new aspect: **The Old Channel**). Behind you, pitch-smoke and Warden torchlight swallow Miller's Row whole, spear-points and screaming fading into the rain as the four of you and the boy slip past unseen, unchallenged, into water only a Weir-Keeper's blood and a toll-keeper's ear could have read safely. Kest's breath still rattles wrong against Anselm's arm, but you've bought him distance from the fire and the chains both — the deep water, for once, was the safer road.

She locks up mid-sentence, eyes gone distant, just long enough for Ossa's hand to twitch back toward his chain-hook and the line of refugees to shift uneasily at her silence.

Lieutenant Vex of the Blackwater Cartel, soaked to the bone and stripped of her usual swagger, corners Anselm at the gate — the debt she owes him has finally come due, and she's calling it in not for coin but for names she loves.

violations.issue: reported fictional trigger fiction:the party enters a settlement that is not an unused fictional trigger

refusal cost not built from a face-up GM tag: {'card_id': 'F-03', 'tag': 'Undermanned and Frightened', 'text': "If Petra refuses this compel, the terrified, understrength Wardens overreact instead — a jumpy patrol torches the tollgate house's outbuilding on mere rumor of blight, and the party has to fight the fire and the panic at once."}

Drawn story cards (CA-06, drawn events 72/73 in Scene 3 and again 97/98 in Scene 4; PE-05, drawn event 116/117 in Scene 5) are never logged as being returned to their pile at scene end. §6A's 'Resolving a story draw' step 3 mandates: 'At scene end, return it and its echo slips to its pile and reshuffle, unless it was retired.' Scene cleanup logs (events 74–80, 99–105, 123–126) show binder returns and rail discards for other card types but no equivalent removal for the story cards, and none were retired.

The draw-trigger table specifies that on a 'player accepts a compel that did not come from a deck draw' story draw, 'the GM gains 1 free invoke on it.' None of the three story draws in the log (events 72–73, 97–98, 116–117) show a corresponding free-invoke grant, unlike every other card-surfacing event in the log (e.g. events 2, 3, 27, 30, 61, 64, 82, 83, 89), which explicitly log 'GM +1 free invoke' or a 'surface' row with 'N free invoke(s).'

ambiguities.issue: In the PLEA FOR HELP beat (event 26), both drawn cards' types (ROOTS→WHO and FACTION→WHO) nominally map to the same single 'WHO' blank, since the frame's only other open blank ('WHERE') isn't in either card's type-to-blank list. The rules don't state which of two simultaneously-drawn cards gets the type-matching blank versus falls through to the 'first open blank still empty' rule.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table resolved cards in draw order: the first card drawn (AN-02, ROOTS) took the matching WHO blank; the second (F-04, FACTION), finding WHO already filled, fell through to the remaining open blank (WHERE) per the fallback clause. Same situation recurred in event 58 (FALSE SANCTUARY), where neither ROOTS (PE-01) nor REACH (CA-04) maps to WHERE/HOW at all, so both fell through in draw order.

ambiguities.issue: Altered scene text is defined as changing 'who is there, the location, or the weather.' The F-03 draw (event 108) instead introduced a new ongoing event/hazard (Wardens actively burning an infected house) rather than swapping an existing who/where/weather element.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table treated 'element' broadly enough to include a new complicating action tied to the drawn tag, rather than restricting Altered scenes strictly to substituting who/where/weather.

ambiguities.issue: The GM anchor card F-02 (non-GLOBAL) is placed face-up during pre-session prep (event 3, scene 0), before any scene formally begins, and is granted a free invoke at that time. §3 says a GM card's free invoke on the rail 'must be used within that scene,' but scene 0 is not a played scene.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The free invoke from the scene-0 anchor placement was treated as usable during the session's first scene (Scene 1).

free_text.best_moment: Reading the water path through Miller's Row while the swarm-song called my name. Petra accepted the compel, got caught in the song's pull, then succeeded with style—and that success had real weight. It combined her core ability (Notice + reading water) with her core conflict (the song's pull), and she won through her own skill, not rescue. It felt like Petra's story.
free_text.most_frustrating: Two things: First, the hidden hive-marked boy reveal. It was excellent storytelling, but I was reacting to Caddock's secret rather than making meaningful choices about it. Second, the S5 compel when the song called Petra's name—refusing it was technically possible but cost a fate point I didn't have, which meant the "choice" was really no choice at all. Felt slightly railroaded into accepting.
free_text.background_used: Well. The toll-gate knowledge, Petra's unique swarm-song hearing, her childhood home—all woven naturally into the story's engine. "Raised at the Ashwater Tollgate" and "Vow to Ring Everyone Home" were central without feeling forced. The weakness on the song (freezes when it calls her name) fired as intended—creates drama without being cheap.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: More agency in the Caddock confrontation—I wanted to push back, investigate her reasoning, have real back-and-forth before accepting the situation. Also wanted to activate more of her relationship background (the Marrows, Vex, her contacts) more actively rather than just being told about debts coming due.
free_text.one_sentence: Petra's backstory felt integrated naturally into the story's stakes without being weaponized unfairly—her abilities and history were the engine, not the obstacle.

free_text.best_moment: Examining the hidden hive-marked child in the loft. For a moment, Anselm's exorcist knowledge actually mattered—he could read the signs with professional precision: the flat eyes, the wrong flush, the patient swarm-song threading thin beneath the boy's breath. It was the closest he got to doing what he came into the world to do.
free_text.most_frustrating: As an exorcist confronted with a hive-marked child and a hive-touched boy being carried through floodwater, Anselm never got to actually *perform* exorcism—no rites, no purification, no moment where his specific skills and calling mattered beyond observation. The narrative momentum swept past the horror and the hard questions into rescue and escape.
free_text.background_used: The Favor compel hit perfectly—Vex's life-debt pulled Anselm into the story organically and personally. The drowning-trauma echo (sister's death paralleling Kest's danger) landed well, and the water-knowledge felt implicit and right. About a quarter of Anselm's cards came into active play. GOOD, but the Saint Orrin lore and the Oath stayed dormant.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Perform actual exorcism work on the discovered child. Sit with the moral weight of what Caddock had hidden—Anselm would have questions about how long the blight sat in that boy, whether any of him was still human, whether hiding it from the Wardens was mercy or complicity. The story moved too fast to let him confront that.
free_text.one_sentence: My background was engaged directly through compel and thematic echo, but I ended up playing support in other people's big moments rather than driving my own character arc.

chronicle.summary:
Fleeing the burning of Miller's Row, the party carried the fevered boy Kest around the Wardens' torches and chains, cutting through deep, hive-haunted water that only a toll-keeper's ear and a Weir-Keeper's blood could read safely. Petra broke the swarm-song's grip on her own name at the last instant, Caddock bulled through the cold current without losing her footing, and Yarrow found the ghost of an old drowned channel that gave the whole party a hidden road to safety. They slipped past Miller's Row unseen and unchallenged, buying Kest distance from both the fire and the Wardens' chains, though his breath still rattles wrong in Anselm's arms as the session closes.</parameter>
